title: The bees and the honey
hookLine: many trees, one honey: one Being under every creature, and each still itself

cards: Pick up a jar of honey. Wildflower, the label says. Bees visited clover, dandelion, an apple tree, a lime tree, and plenty of flowers no one will ever list.
They brought it all home and worked it together into one golden thing. Try to find the apple-tree part. You can't.
It's not gone; it's in there. It just can't be picked out anymore. Uddalaka, teaching his son, picks up the same jar.

teach.b: Just as bees make honey, my dear, Uddalaka says, by gathering the juices of many different trees and bringing them to a single sweetness, and in the honey those juices can't tell one another, I am the juice of this tree, I am the juice of that tree, in the same way all these creatures, when they merge into Being, don't know: we have merged into Being.
Then a line that's easy to skip, and shouldn't be.

teach.h: NO JUICE SAYS: I'M FROM THIS TREE.
teach.b: Whatever they are in this world, a tiger, a lion, a wolf, a boar, a worm, a moth, a gnat, a mosquito, they become that again. So hold both halves.
Underneath, the separate names are gone: one Being, which later teachers call Brahman, under every creature.

teach.h: THE TIGER WAKES UP A TIGER.
teach.b: And here, in the world, the tiger wakes up a tiger and the mosquito a mosquito. That's the Hindu teaching in this jar: one reality under everything that lives, and each life still truly itself.
It's one reason Hindu teachers ask you to see the sacred in every creature, not just the ones you like.
The kid at school who gets on your nerves, the neighbor's barking dog, the mosquito at your ear: different jars, the same sweetness underneath.
Then, once again, the refrain: that subtle essence is the self of all this; that is the truth; that is the self; you are that, Shvetaketu. Please, sir, says the son, tell me more.

how: Vedanta teachers often take Uddalaka's lessons one at a time, as here, and the honey image is one of several the Chandogya uses for creatures merging into Being in sleep and death.

o: a spring flower the bees love most of all
a bell rung at the start of a lesson
honey: many juices made into one sweetness

games.q: what's inside the lesson — tap the pairs.
p: can't say which tree they're from

s: in Uddalaka's lesson, merged creatures know they've merged into Being
no juice says it; no creature knows we have merged.
Uddalaka says creatures come back as what they were
a tiger, a lion, a wolf, a gnat: they become that again.
the lesson ends with the refrain you are that
tat tvam asi, again, and Shvetaketu asks for more.

games.q: a friend says: Hindus think we're all one, so nobody is really themselves. what does the honey lesson say?
o: right: in this lesson, the tiger stops being a tiger.
both: one Being underneath, and in the world the tiger wakes up a tiger.
wrong: nothing at all connects one creature to another.
games.why: in the honey, no juice says which tree it came from. yet, Uddalaka says, whatever they are here, they become that again. one Being, many real lives.

practice: Pick out the separate sounds around you one at a time, a fan, a car outside, a voice, your own breath, and name each one.
Then, breath by breath, stop naming them, and let them run together into one sound, no part saying where it came from.

wordCard.voice: Madhu, honey, sweetness. Many juices, one sweetness: in Being, no creature says I came from this tree, and in the world, each comes back as itself.

orig.note: Sanskrit madhu: honey, sweetness. the bees make madhu from many trees.

carryVoice: Your line: one Being under every name, and every name still itself. Tomorrow, the rivers. See you then.

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 6.9.1–4 (the bees and the honey; the returning creatures; the refrain)
